questions.prompt: Four agent branches were all cut from the same `main`. While they ran, `main` gained two commits. You merge them in the order the agents finished. Two merges conflict even though each agent touched a different function. What is the cause?
options: The agents disagreed about the same lines and the conflict is real
`git merge` always conflicts above three branches
Each branch was cut from a base that `main` has since moved past, so the merges are reconciling against different starting points
The worktrees share an object store, which corrupts the merges
questions.explanation: Merging stale, unrebalanced branches forces each merge to reconcile a different old base; rebasing all of them onto the current `main` first removes the conflict. Option A is the tempting wrong answer because a conflict *looks* like disagreement — but these are different functions, so the agents never contested anything. Git has no three-branch conflict limit, and a shared object store is normal, not corrupting.

questions.prompt: You have three finished agent branches and `main` has moved once. Which sequence best matches the strategy in this lesson?
options: Rebase each branch onto today's `main`, then merge them in creation order
Merge each branch as-is, oldest base first, no rebase
Rebase `main` onto each agent branch in turn
Squash all three branches into one commit and merge that
questions.explanation: Rebasing each private branch onto the current `main` gives every branch the same base before it merges, and creation order keeps history readable. Option C is the tempting wrong answer because it mentions the right verb — but you rebase the *branch you own* onto `main`, never `main` onto the branch. Merging stale branches is what produces phantom conflicts, and squashing throws away attribution for no reason here.

questions.prompt: An agent finished an important branch on Monday. `main` moved four times before Friday. The agent's code is unchanged and correct. What grew over those four days, and who pays for it?
options: The agent's work — it silently becomes stale and needs a re-run
Nothing — a branch that is not rebased never changes cost
The object store — worktree branches bloat the repository over time
The rebase — you pay, because you reconcile four days of `main` movement against a branch cut from Monday
questions.explanation: The work stays correct; the *integration* cost grows with every commit `main` gains, and that cost lands on whoever merges. Option B is the tempting wrong answer because it is true that the branch's files do not change — the work is fine — but the rebase against a moved `main` gets larger and more conflict-prone. Branches do not bloat the object store and are not auto-re-run.

questions.prompt: After rebasing and merging an agent branch, you want history to clearly show that this batch of agent work arrived together, even though a fast-forward is possible. What do you do?
options: Merge normally and rely on the commit timestamps
Merge with `--no-ff` to force a merge commit
Rebase the branch a second time
Add a tag pointing at the branch tip
questions.explanation: `--no-ff` forces a merge commit with two parents, which records the join even when the label could just slide forward. Option A is the tempting wrong answer because timestamps are visible in the log and feel like a record — but a fast-forward leaves no node, so nothing marks the batch. A second rebase changes nothing and a tag is not part of the merge.
